s: A Site for the Hydrogen Bomb
t: In 1950 the Atomic Energy Commission was expanding the nation's production of material for nuclear weapons, and it asked the Du Pont company to build and run new reactors to make it. In June, with war begun in Korea, the order grew to five heavy-water reactors (WB: SRS at Fifty ch. 7). The project became the Savannah River Plant, renamed the Savannah River Site in 1989 (WB: srs.gov 1980s).

s: A Site for the Hydrogen Bomb
t: Du Pont surveyed candidate sites and settled on the middle Savannah River in South Carolina, a tract big enough to hold an exclusion zone around the reactors (WB: ch. 7). DOE's own timeline dates President Truman's letter to Du Pont to October 20, 1950 (WB: DOE, energy.gov/srs).

s: A Site for the Hydrogen Bomb
t: The announcement came at noon on November 28, 1950: about 250,000 acres in Aiken and Barnwell counties, to be called the Savannah River Plant, designed, built and operated by Du Pont (WB: SRS at Fifty ch. 8). The next morning it was in the Atlanta Constitution (IA) and in newspapers as far away as Victoria, British Columbia (IA).

The land was not empty. It held small, rural farming communities. Most of the farms were worked by tenants, and most of the farm workers were African American (WB: ch. 7). The largest town, Ellenton, had about 600 people; it began as a railroad station in 1873 (WB: ch. 7; WB: SRARP, 1996). Dunbarton, with 231 people, was a railroad town incorporated in 1910 (WB: ch. 7; WB: SRARP, 1993).

Smaller settlements, among them Meyers Mill, Hawthorne, Robbins, Leigh and Hattieville, were mostly stops on the railroad. Du Pont moved the boundary to leave out two others, Jackson and Snelling (WB: ch. 7). Ellenton had a violent past: in 1876, during Reconstruction, armed white rifle clubs marched on Black militia there in what became known as the Ellenton riot (WB: SRARP). A state historical marker for the town of Ellenton stands on Highway 64 at Barnwell (WB: Historical Marker Database).

How many people were moved depends on who is counting. The first press release spoke of about 1,500 families; early reports said up to 8,000 farmers; the AEC (Atomic Energy Commission) settled on 6,000 people in 1,500 families (WB: ch. 8). The Savannah River Archaeological Research Program later put it at about 5,000 (WB: SRARP).

The process of acquiring the land was run by the Army Corps of Engineers, with residents of the first area gone by March 15, 1951, and of the second by June 1. Landowners who disputed their land appraisal went to federal condemnation proceedings. At least 4,500 graves had to be moved (WB: ch. 8). By late 1951 the government was acquiring 265 tracts in Ellenton alone (DL).

Owners objected to how their land was bought. A congressional staff report in late 1951 found Ellenton residents told to be gone by February 1952, while their property was still unappraised. Each owner was given a single offer at the appraised value. Those who took the first offer were as much as 20 percent worse off than those who held out. About a hundred owners met twice to protest the prices.

The Atomic Energy Commission answered that most condemnations came from defects in title rather than price: owners who could not show clear legal ownership, often because land had passed to many heirs, or who could not be found. Of 169 cases it listed, 39 were over price and 130 over title, It conceded that juries in seven contested cases had awarded substantially more than the government's appraisal (DL).

The magazine The Reporter brought the story to the nation in March 1951, when it reported on the quiet doom of Ellenton (IA). Jet told a different part of it that December, focusing on Black families moving whole houses fifteen miles to New Ellenton, the replacement town. Its photograph ran under the heading "H-Bomb Victims" (IA). A 1965 federal housing study counted about 30 white and 120 Black families relocated near New Ellenton (IA), and by 1953 Congress was hearing that New Ellenton had been left out of aid it needed (DL).

The displaced spoke for themselves decades later, in oral histories collected from 1990 and published as Memories of Home for Ellenton and for Dunbarton and Meyers Mill (WB: OSTI 272945; WB: OSTI 10171577). The program's web pages and the chapter PDFs survive in Wayback; srarp.org itself is gone (WB; WB: Ellenton volume).

James McBride's life of James Brown traces part of the singer's family to Ellenton, where relatives "cared for one another's children" (IA). Louise Cassels's The Unexpected Exodus (1971), the classic memoir of the leaving, is cataloged in Open Library, though it has no copy to read or borrow yet (OL: Open Library).
Follow this thread, the displaced towns. Continues in Chapter 3, The Plant's Museum.

According to the Natural Resources Defense Council, construction began on reactors in 1951 (reactor R in June, P in July, L in October) (IA). The Bureau of Labor Statistics followed the work force in a 1952 study (IA: part I). It records Black tenant farmers arriving in Augusta looking for jobs in May 1951. At an NAACP (National Association for the Advancement of Colored People) meeting in Aiken that September, speakers accused Du Pont and an Augusta union of keeping Black workers out of skilled jobs, and said they had enough evidence to go to court.

Getting hired was a fight of its own. In November 1951 a House labor subcommittee under Graham Barden held five days of hearings in Augusta on charges that union membership had become a condition of work (DL).

Its report the next year found that Du Pont hired manual labor through a verbal understanding with the AFL (American Federation of Labor) building-trades unions, turning job seekers away at the gate, and that Atomic Energy Commission officials had either approved or failed to find out (DL). In November 1952 pickets from an AFL engineers' union nearly stopped construction, with about 25,000 other workers honoring the line (IA).

The same system kept Black workers out of the skilled trades. The National Urban League's field notes, filed with the Barden hearings, record that it pressed Du Pont in August 1951 over its failure to hire Black electricians, mechanics, plumbers, welders and ironworkers. Company officials replied that as long as the unions could supply the workers, they would hire from no other source. Apart from 116 Black carpenters, they would not say how many Black workers they employed (DL). When Truman created a committee on government contract compliance that December, Jet expected the Savannah River contractors to be among its first targets (IA).

Housing the workers was its own crisis. In February 1951 Congress held a hearing in Aiken. It expected construction to peak around the start of 1953 (DL). A year later, in February 1952, the mayors of New Ellenton and Augusta testified about dormitories and about Du Pont's part in housing workers (DL).

House & Home reported about 4,000 trailers for married workers (IA). The housing builder later sued Du Pont in a case that reached the Supreme Court (DL), and South Carolina's attempt to tax Du Pont's work on the plant set out what a government-owned, contractor-operated plant was in law (DL).

Du Pont wrote its own record of all this, volume by volume, in construction and design histories now on OSTI (Office of Scientific and Technical Information) (WB: OSTI 10159481; WB: OSTI 10151705). The company's administrative files are at the Hagley Museum and Library (WB: DOE finding aid).

The 305-M test pile was the first reactor on the site to start up, in 1952, the year heavy-water production began in D Area (WB: srs.gov 1950s). R reactor started up in December 1953, P on February 20, 1954, and all five were running by the end of March 1955 (WB: SRS at Fifty ch. 11).

The separations plants took the irradiated fuel and targets from the reactors, dissolved them, and used chemistry to pull out the plutonium and other products, leaving the radioactive waste behind. F Area was the world's first full-scale plant to use this method, called Purex, and purified plutonium; H Area mostly recovered enriched uranium (WB: ch. 11).

F Area started in 1954 and H Area in 1955. Radioactive tritium went to the AEC (Atomic Energy Commission) from 1955, and the basic plant was complete in 1956 (WB: srs.gov 1950s; WB: History Highlights). The first shipment of radioactive plutonium is dated December 1954 by one official source and 1955 by others (WB: ch. 11; WB).

P reactor also served pure science. In 1955 and 1956 two Los Alamos physicists, Frederick Reines and Clyde Cowan, set up detectors beside it (WB: SRS at Fifty ch. 13). Reactors give off huge numbers of neutrinos, tiny particles with no electric charge that pass through almost everything (WB: Nobel Prize, 1995). In June 1956 they announced the first detection of the neutrino (WB: ch. 13). Reines shared the 1995 Nobel Prize in Physics for it; Cowan had died by then (WB: Nobel Prize).

Then demand for weapons materials fell. R reactor shut down in 1964 and L in 1968, both because less nuclear material was needed (DL: Senate hearing, 1983; WB: srs.gov 1960s). The heavy-water components test reactor also closed in December 1964, for a different reason: the AEC was turning away from heavy-water power reactors, and it was never restarted (WB: ch. 13).

The plant's own figures understated its early releases. The CDC's (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's) dose reconstruction found that the radioactive iodine-131 released to the air in the 1950s, mainly from the separations plants, was about four times what the site had reported. That was largely because its samplers caught only one chemical form of the iodine (WB: CDC dose reconstruction, Phase II ch. 1). The largest tritium releases to the air came in 1957–59 from the H Area tritium facilities (WB).

A fuel failure in R reactor in November 1957 sent more than 1,900 curies of radioactivity into a seepage basin dug only that year. In 1958 three high-level waste tanks in H Area leaked through their steel walls (WB: CDC Phase II ch. 5).

The final report judged the doses to people living nearby small, but found that a child born in 1955 received much of a lifetime dose from the site in its first years, from those early iodine releases (WB: CDC Phase III).

On March 14, 1955, after a light rain, contamination across the plant set off the shoe monitors of workers coming in from outside. The plant blamed fallout from a bomb test in Nevada two days before. In 1985 Bernd Franke and Robert Alvarez argued that a reactor accident was the likelier source, since the contamination centered on the K, L and P reactors (WB: CDC Phase II ch. 6).

At Senator Thurmond's request, the staff of the Senate Armed Services Committee investigated and reported in July 1986 that their case was "merely speculative": the contamination matched fallout from Teapot Hornet, an above-ground atomic bomb test at the Nevada Test Site two days before, and the plant's own monitoring showed no release (DL). The CDC's contractor judged Nevada fallout highly probable, while noting that the full extent of the deposit would never be known (WB: CDC Phase II ch. 6).

The workers' side of the reckoning came later still. In 2012 the government added everyone who had worked at the site for at least 250 days between 1953 and 1972 to the Special Exposure Cohort of the federal occupational illness compensation program. Their cancer claims no longer turn on reconstructing each worker's dose (WB: NIOSH).

For the towns around it, the plant was an economic boom with an environmental cost. It brought jobs, newcomers, new schools and federal money. It also brought the radioactive releases described earlier, and the damage to streams and wildlife told in SRS and Ecology. Later chapters follow what that meant for the people who fish the river and drink its water (Chapter 3).

The plant brought thousands of newcomers to a rural area. At a Senate hearing in Aiken in February 1952, the AEC's (Atomic Energy Commission's) local manager said there would be no government town like Oak Ridge or Richland; private builders would house the workers. He counted 3,000 trailers already in private courts, and new classrooms paid for through the federal Office of Education (DL: Senate hearing, 1952).

Aiken had 7,167 people in 1950 and told the same hearing it expected metropolitan Aiken to reach 20,000 by 1955. It asked for federal help with about $2.6 million of the $2.9 million in new water, sewer, police and fire services it said it needed (DL).

A Labor Department study found more than 10,000 workers had moved into the area by November 1951. School enrollment rose 69 percent in Williston, some Barnwell County schools ran double shifts, and under segregation one town put off building a needed school for Black children while it waited for federal money (IA: Monthly Labor Review, 1952).
From 1954 the government paid Aiken, Barnwell and Allendale counties in place of the property taxes the site's land no longer paid (WB: DOE, 2008).
Follow this thread, the towns and their economy. Continues in Chapter 2, Living with the Plant; Chapter 3, Living with the Plant; Chapter 4, Living with the Plant.

Before the reactors ran, the river was surveyed. Ruth Patrick of the Academy of Natural Sciences made a baseline survey in 1951 (WB: srs.gov 1950s), and the Public Health Service sampled the river's water and its natural radioactivity in 1951–52 (IA; IA).

In 1951 the AEC (Atomic Energy Commission) asked the University of Georgia and the University of South Carolina to survey the land's plants and animals before construction began, offering each about $10,000 a year (WB: SRS at Fifty ch. 17). The Georgia team was led by Eugene Odum, whose 1953 textbook Fundamentals of Ecology made him known as the "father of modern ecosystem ecology" (WB: ch. 17; IA; IA).

Georgia's survey grew into a research program. Its Laboratory of Radiation Ecology, with a staff of 15, exposed plants and animals to controlled doses of radiation to learn what it does to them in the wild (WB: ch. 17). The work became a permanent laboratory in 1961 (WB: srs.gov 1960s) — the Savannah River Ecology Laboratory, run by the University of Georgia, which dates its own founding to 1951 (WB: SREL). In the 1960s its scientists were, in the official history's words, "at the heart of" the new idea of the ecosystem: what one is and how it works (WB: ch. 17).

Much of the land had been worked hard. When the government took it, about two-thirds was forest, most of it already logged, and a third was cropland or pasture (IA: SREL scientists, 2002). In 1952 the AEC and the U.S. Forest Service agreed to manage the land together, and the Forest Service's first job was planting trees "by the thousands" on old farms (DL: Forest Service, 1995).

The site and its reactors changed the local streams and watershed. Lower Three Runs Creek was dammed in 1958 to make Par Pond, a cooling reservoir, and the reactors sent hot water down creeks such as Steel Creek (IA: L-Reactor environmental impact statement, 1984).

By the end of the 1960s the plant had done what it was built for. Its reactors had made plutonium and tritium for more than a decade, and two of them had already closed as demand fell (Running the Plant). Its land had also become a place to study, with forests replanted, ecologists at work and a record of what it released. The 1970s brought new environmental laws and a public that wanted to know more, and the plant came under scrutiny, as Chapter 2 tells.
Follow this thread, the land and its wildlife. Continues in Chapter 2, SRS and Ecology; Chapter 3, SRS and Ecology; Chapter 3, The Laboratories; Chapter 4, Ecology and the SRS.

Through the 1970s the plant reported its releases. Du Pont's semiannual monitoring summaries were reprinted in the federal Radiation Data and Reports (DL), and its annual environmental reports run from 1974 on OSTI (Office of Scientific and Technical Information) (WB: OSTI 4174736). In 1972 the plant became the first National Environmental Research Park (WB: srs.gov 1970s); see SRS and Ecology.

Radioactive tritium was the plant's largest routine release, averaging more than half a million curies a year to the air in 1974–77 (WB: OSTI 6206385). Single accidents added to it. On May 2, 1974, some 479,000 curies of tritium gas escaped from a stack (WB: OSTI 7100365), a release a Lawrence Livermore report on the national emergency-response system's tracking of it called a small quantity, not dangerous to the public (WB: OSTI 7282426).

In September 1984 another 43,800 curies, mostly tritium oxide, drifted toward New Ellenton and Aiken (WB: OSTI 6417935), and on July 31, 1987, a further 172,000 curies were released (WB: OSTI 7130595).

Downstream, the plant tested the tritium in the drinking water every month at the Beaufort-Jasper Water Authority in South Carolina and the Port Wentworth plant in Georgia. It also screened the 865 deer and 8 hogs killed in its 1971 hunt for radioactive cesium-137 before releasing them to hunters (DL).
The hunts still go on today; see Chapter 4.
Follow this thread, radioactivity in the river and its animals. Continues in Chapter 3, The Neighbors and the River; Chapter 4, Ecology and the SRS.

However, the Reagan-era buildup of nuclear weapons needed more plutonium. In 1982 the plant lowered the Pu-240 content of its product to blend with Hanford's (WB: SRS at Fifty ch. 19), and DOE (Department of Energy) moved to restart L reactor, idle since 1968, on an environmental assessment rather than a full impact statement (WB: OSTI 5060401).

The Natural Resources Defense Council sued. On July 15, 1983, the district court held that restarting L reactor required an environmental impact statement and ordered DOE to prepare one (WB: the court's decision). It did not halt the restart: a law reporter's summary says the court refused a preliminary injunction (WB: Environmental Law Reporter), while the decision set South Carolina's request for one for a later hearing. The Senate Armed Services Committee had already held a field hearing in North Augusta that February (DL).

At that hearing Senator Mattingly of Georgia said his state was firmly against burying the plant's high-level waste in the bedrock beneath the site. He warned it could contaminate the Tuscaloosa aquifer, a deep layer of water-bearing ground that he called the main source of water for Georgia. DOE assured him it would not propose bedrock burial again. The Natural Resources Defense Council's witness pointed to cesium contamination off the site, just downstream of where Steel Creek enters the river (DL).

South Carolina and Georgia had both opposed bedrock disposal (IA). The final EIS came in May 1984 (WB: DOE); it and the other impact statements of the period are gathered in one archive.org upload (IA). L restarted in 1985. C reactor shut down that year, permanently from 1986 (WB: srs.gov 1980s).

Outside critics read the record differently from the operator. Deadly Crop in the Tank Farm (1986) assessed the high-level waste tanks (WB: IEER); Du Pont published a rebuttal (WB: OSTI 5881523). The Washington Post described aging reactors carrying the buildup, one down for a cracked vessel — a clipping that survives in the CIA's (Central Intelligence Agency's) files (IA).

What the plant had poured into its seepage basins came back through the groundwater. Reviewing permit applications in 1981, South Carolina's health and environment department judged that the volumes sent to the basins strongly suggested groundwater problems; in 1983 the plant reported that a well supplying drinking water to its own employees was contaminated, and two more followed (DL).
The department's deputy commissioner told Senator Glenn's committee in 1987 that plant staff had at first been reluctant to accept the state's regulatory authority (DL).

GAO (General Accounting Office) found solvents in the groundwater under the M Area fuel plant at more than 30,000 times proposed drinking-water standards. Tritium at the separations areas was more than 2,500 times the standard. DOE answered that the contamination stayed under federal land and posed no threat to the public (IA: GAO 1986).

By 1991 the Office of Technology Assessment reported an EPA (Environmental Protection Agency) finding that the pump-and-treat system meant to clean the M Area plume was not adequately designed to reach its goal (DL).

A National Academy of Sciences panel reviewed safety at the defense production reactors for DOE (Department of Energy) in 1987 (IA). Du Pont announced that year that it would not stay on as operator (WB: srs.gov 1980s). In February 1988 a Senate subcommittee heard DOE, the plant manager and Du Pont on why L reactor's power had been cut (IA).

That year an internal list of thirty significant reactor incidents became public. The official history presents the report as meant to show safety improving (WB: ch. 19); the Senate investigator who obtained it remembers it as evidence of concealment (WB: Alliance for Nuclear Accountability).

The reactors went down one after another — K in April, L in June, P in August — over emergency cooling concerns (WB: ch. 19). On September 30, 1988, the General Accounting Office told Senator Glenn's and Representative Synar's committees how P reactor's start-up had gone ahead despite a reactivity shortfall larger than any the plant had seen (DL; WB: gao.gov).

Glenn's bill to put the weapons plants under outside safety oversight was already in hearings (DL). The next day, October 1, the New York Times put the story on its front page. It reported severe accidents at all five reactors, kept secret for up to 31 years. They were documented in a 19-page memorandum from a plant supervisor to his superiors at Du Pont (WB: New York Times). By November the paper was asking how Congress had missed the signs (WB: New York Times).

In April 1989 the Westinghouse Savannah River Company took over from Du Pont (WB: ch. 19). The same year the Savannah River Plant became the Savannah River Site and went on the National Priorities List (WB: srs.gov 1980s). GAO's (General Accounting Office's) 1989 testimony set the site inside a complex-wide picture of cleanup and modernization problems (DL).

DOE still meant to restart. In February 1991 it planned K for that summer and L for 1992, at $3.2 billion for restart and operations (WB: GAO RCED-91-95), and issued safety evaluations for K (WB: OSTI 5625511). In December 1991 tritium from K reactor reached the Savannah River (WB: OSTI 5281815; WB: OSTI 10179303).

GAO had warned in 1989 that DOE had only begun to address earthquake weaknesses that had existed at the site for years. It also found that the seismic review behind P reactor's 1988 restart used a less stringent standard than the Nuclear Regulatory Commission's (IA: GAO 1989).

In March 1991 a depression was found on the downstream face of the Par Pond dam. That summer the site lowered the reservoir about 19 feet. This exposed some 1,300 acres of cesium-contaminated sediment and sent tritium and cesium into the river (WB: OSTI 7247383). The exposed bed became a Superfund interim action (WB: OSTI 10192315).
A 1998 DOE notice dates the leak to 1992 (DL). In 1992 K was started up for a test run and was then shut down permanently (WB: srs.gov 1990s). Bomb making at Savannah River was over.

What it had released was reconstructed later. The CDC's (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's) dose reconstruction counted about 3,000 release incidents involving tritium between 1954 and 1992 (WB: CDC Phase II).

The plant was the area's anchor employer. A 1984 Energy Department report put its permanent workforce at 9,200 in December 1982, most of them working for Du Pont, with plant workers and their families making up about half of Aiken's 15,000 people. The same report found that Aiken and Richmond counties ranked in the top half nationally for income in 1974, while most counties around the plant ranked in the bottom 11 percent (IA: DOE, 1984).

The 1980s buildup brought the workforce to 18,635 by May 1989, and a 1990 DOE study said shutting the K, L and P reactors would cost about 9,600 jobs (IA: DOE, 1990). In 1992 South Carolina listed Westinghouse Savannah River, with 23,000 workers, as its largest manufacturing employer, and noted that federal cutbacks had begun (IA: South Carolina Economic Report, 1993).

The plant's neighbors and workers also raised questions about their health. In August 1989 Senator Glenn argued that DOE's research on the health of its own workers had been subordinated to production. Senator Kohl called for removing the apparent conflict of interest, and said he was open to moving that research to Health and Human Services. The record included a 1988 study that reported a significant excess of leukemia deaths among hourly Savannah River workers hired before 1955 (IA: Senate hearing, 1989). The later dose reconstruction was run by the CDC (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention) (WB: CDC).

Studies of the neighbors began at the same time. A July 1990 National Institutes of Health survey compared cancer deaths in Aiken and Barnwell counties and Georgia's Burke County with similar counties elsewhere. It found no excess among children, more leukemia at ages 20 to 39 and slightly more lung cancer in older adults, and said it did not show cancer excesses tied to the plant (DL; DL).

s: An Emerging Environmental Movement Impacts SRS
t: A new environmental movement changed the rules for the plant. The National Environmental Policy Act, signed in January 1970, required federal projects to study their effects on the environment in public impact statements (WB: SRS at Fifty, pp. 474–75). In December 1970 a reorganization created the Environmental Protection Agency, which took over the federal journal that reprinted the plant's radiation monitoring (DL). In December 1974 the EPA issued the plant its first water-discharge permit (WB: SRS at Fifty, pp. 480–81).

s: An Emerging Environmental Movement Impacts SRS
t: By the late 1970s many environmentalists had also turned against nuclear power. Near the plant their anger focused on two projects: a plant to recycle plutonium from power-reactor fuel at Barnwell, built on land cut from the site's eastern edge, and Georgia Power's planned nuclear plant at Waynesboro, Georgia (WB: SRS at Fifty, pp. 482–83).

s: An Emerging Environmental Movement Impacts SRS
t: The Three Mile Island accident in Pennsylvania on March 28, 1979 (DL) gave the movement new force. Small protests at Savannah River had come and gone through the decade; the largest came that year. About 1,500 people joined a three-day protest of seminars, marches and a concert by Graham Nash. It ended with 162 arrests for trespassing at the plant, the Barnwell plant and a nearby radioactive-waste dump, 30 of them at Savannah River (WB: SRS at Fifty, p. 482). The site dates its years of anti-nuclear protest from then (WB: srs.gov 1970s).

s: An Emerging Environmental Movement Impacts SRS
t: The Reagan-era buildup brought the protests to the plant's gates. In late May 1982, 500 to 700 people rallied near the plant for a freeze on nuclear weapons (IA: Florida Flambeau, June 3, 1982).

s: An Emerging Environmental Movement Impacts SRS
t: These protests ran alongside the official challenges told elsewhere in this chapter: the lawsuit over restarting L reactor (L-Reactor comes back) and the investigations of 1988 (1987–1988: the reactors stop).

In 1972 the site became the first National Environmental Research Park (WB: srs.gov 1970s). The ecology laboratory's work on reactor cooling water began in 1969, once satellite imagery had made the water temperatures impossible to keep secret (WB: Ecological Society of America), and became the Thermal Ecology symposia (IA).

The cooling water did real damage. A 1987 environmental impact statement found that K reactor's hot water had altered 670 acres of forested wetland along Pen Branch. C reactor's had altered about 1,147 acres, some 60 percent, along Four Mile Creek, where open water and marsh had replaced hardwood forest (IA: DOE, 1987). Restarting L reactor meant sending hot water into the Steel Creek swamp again (DL: Senate hearing, 1983).

Wildlife was in trouble too. In 1984 the wood stork was listed as endangered, and the L-Reactor study recorded 102 of them feeding near the Steel Creek delta the summer before (IA: DOE, 1984). In 1985 the site's red-cockaded woodpeckers were down to four birds; at DOE's (Department of Energy's) request, Forest Service scientists began carving artificial nest cavities and moving birds in from other forests (DL: Forest Service).
Follow this thread, the land and its wildlife. Earlier: Chapter 1, SRS and Ecology. Continues in Chapter 3, SRS and Ecology; Chapter 3, The Laboratories; Chapter 4, Ecology and the SRS.

The official history marks the turn plainly: the mission became environmental management, not production (WB: SRS at Fifty ch. 20). DOE (Department of Energy) priced the complex-wide legacy in Estimating the Cold War Mortgage (IA) and traced each waste stream to the process that made it in Linking Legacies (IA). In October 2003 the last spent fuel left the receiving basin, closing what the site called a forty-year era (WB).

Spent fuel kept arriving as well as leaving. The United States moved to take back the fuel it had supplied to research reactors abroad. In 1994 GAO (General Accounting Office) reported that delays had already led reactors in Belgium and Germany to reprocess theirs, and that DOE meant to store the first returns at Savannah River (IA: GAO 1994).

DOE's 1996 decision accepted about 22,700 fuel elements from 41 countries over 13 years, most landing at the Charleston Naval Weapons Station, with the aluminum-based fuel all managed at Savannah River (DL: Federal Register, 1996). South Carolina's governor took DOE to court over it (DL).

The largest legacy was liquid: about 36 million gallons in 49 tanks, roughly 421 million curies (WB: DWPF fact sheet). The Defense Waste Processing Facility, built from 1983 and troubled before it ran (IA: GAO 1992), began turning that waste into glass on March 12, 1996 (WB).

Getting the waste into the glass plant was harder. In 1983 DOE chose a process called In-Tank Precipitation to pull radioactive cesium out of the tanks' salt. It was expected to cost $32 million and be finished by 1988. After about a decade and almost half a billion dollars, it was abandoned in 1998 because it gave off large amounts of benzene (DL: House hearing, 2000; WB: GAO).

Its replacement, the Salt Waste Processing Facility, was to be built by 2008 for $900 million; in 2015 DOE's Inspector General reported about $1.4 billion in cost growth and a start no earlier than December 2018 (WB: DOE Inspector General). It poured its 4,000th canister on December 31, 2015, of about 8,000 expected (WB).

Tanks 17 and 20 were closed in 1997, the first in the nation (WB). What could be left in the ground was settled by Section 3116 of the 2005 defense authorization act (WB: govinfo), which Senator Graham said he wrote and which passed by a single vote (WB), and which the National Academies reviewed for Savannah River (IA).
Tanks 18 and 19 followed in 2012 (WB).

In 2018 and 2019 DOE reinterpreted "high-level waste" to turn on how radioactive a waste is rather than where it came from, revising the change after objections from the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, members of Congress and states. Savannah River was its first test: in 2020 DOE decided to send grouted wastewater from the glass plant to a commercial disposal site in Andrews, Texas, beginning with 8 gallons (WB: Federal Register; WB: Federal Register).

In March 2008 the site put up South Carolina historic markers for P and R, the first inside the fence (WB). Then Recovery Act money arrived.

Deactivation of the R reactor building was cleared in March 2009 (WB); the reactors were sealed in place between October 2009 and September 2011 (WB: OSTI 1032952), five years ahead of the schedule without the stimulus (WB). The release marking the end of that work is gone from srs.gov; the Wayback capture is the copy (WB).

MOX (mixed oxide fuel) was a plan to turn surplus weapons plutonium into fuel for commercial nuclear power reactors, so it could no longer be used in bombs (DL: House hearing, 2006). South Carolina's fight over radioactive plutonium began before MOX. In April 2002 DOE (Department of Energy) decided to store surplus plutonium from Rocky Flats at Savannah River. Governor Jim Hodges sued, then issued an executive order banning plutonium from the state's roads, and in June a federal court barred him from interfering with the shipments; the Fourth Circuit found that DOE had not broken environmental law (DL: Hodges v. Abraham). He had vowed to lie in the road to stop them (IA).

Congress spent a decade on turning surplus plutonium into reactor fuel at Savannah River (DL; DL). DOE's 2016 baseline put the mixed-oxide plant at $17.17 billion, finished in 2048 — a document since removed from the watchdog site that posted it (WB: SRS Watch).

South Carolina sued to hold the government to its promises (WB: complaint), and The Post and Courier's source documents on the fight are on archive.org (IA). In May 2018 DOE certified that diluting and disposing of the plutonium would cost less than half of finishing MOX; the Fourth Circuit lifted the injunction keeping the project alive on January 8, 2019 (WB: 4th Cir.).

MOX workers had already been offered a job fair in December 2018 (WB). By August 2019 DOE reported a metric ton of plutonium removed from the state (WB: SC Attorney General). Half of that ton had gone, secretly, to Nevada.

DOE announced in August 2018 that it planned to send up to a metric ton there; Nevada sued, and learned through the suit that DOE had already shipped half of it while seemingly negotiating in good faith. In a 2020 settlement DOE agreed to remove that half ton from Nevada by the end of 2026 and to send no more (WB: Nevada Attorney General).

The site was also offered other countries' material. In 2014 DOE began assessing whether to take Germany's spent pebble-bed reactor fuel: graphite spheres containing American-supplied highly enriched uranium (WB: Federal Register). The site's own Citizens Advisory Board voted against it in 2017 (WB: CAB). By 2022 the German state concerned had chosen to store it at home instead (WB: SRS Watch).

Plutonium from a Japanese research assembly did come, through Charleston in 2016 (WB: SRS Watch). In 2021 NNSA (National Nuclear Security Administration) dropped its plan to send it on to New Mexico. It decided instead to process the plutonium at Savannah River and store it there until a geologic repository exists (WB: Federal Register).
The site's weapons work never fully ended. Work with radioactive tritium continued throughout (WB).

In 2019 the Defense Nuclear Facilities Safety Board warned that a fire, crane drop or explosion in the tritium facilities could cause acute radiation sickness or death in a significant number of people (WB: Federal Register). NNSA's administrator replied, "I do not accept Recommendation 2019-2" (WB: Federal Register).

Compensation for the plant's sick workers came slowly. At a 2003 House hearing Representative Charlie Norwood of Georgia said more than 300 of his constituents had filed claims over work at the site, and only a handful had a decision. The building trades' statement said Savannah River workers were treated unfairly under the program (DL: House hearing, 2003).

The 2012 class that spared early workers individual dose reconstruction was extended in 2021 to subcontracted construction workers through 1990 (WB: Federal Register) and in 2026 through 1993 (EXT: Federal Register).

Studies of the workers kept finding leukemia. A 1995 Oak Ridge study found that the site's workers died at lower rates than the general public but had significantly more leukemia (WB: site epidemiology summary). In 2007 NIOSH (National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health)-funded researchers following 18,883 workers hired from 1950 to 1986 found leukemia risk rising with recorded radiation dose, and excess cancer of the lung lining, often linked to asbestos (WB: NIOSH).

The records behind the claims had gaps. In 2007 NIOSH found that the site had not sent neutron radiation data for some claims (WB: NIOSH). That November a petition asked to add every worker from 1950 to 2007 to the Special Exposure Cohort; the special classes for the site came from it (WB: NIOSH).

Follow this thread, health of workers and neighbors. Earlier: Chapter 1, Radioactive Releases; Chapter 2, Living with the Plant. Continues in Chapter 3, The Neighbors and the River; Chapter 4, Sick Workers and the River Today.

The Medical University of South Carolina ran a cancer and birth-defects registry from 1991 to 1995 for the counties around the site and down the river to Savannah. Some cancers were elevated, among them cervical cancer in Black women and esophageal cancer in Black men, but officials saw no sign they were related to the site (WB: 2002 summary).

In 2007 the federal Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry (ATSDR) found "no apparent public health hazard" from groundwater or surface water leaving the site (WB: ATSDR). An advocacy group, the Radiation and Public Health Project, disagreed in 2012, reporting that 46 of 48 radiation-sensitive disease measures in five nearby counties had risen faster than national rates (WB: advocacy report).

Fishing on the site itself and some surrounding areas is prohibited, with warning signs posted. A 1997 survey of 258 people fishing the river near the site found they ate about 3.2 pounds of fish a month, Black men nearly twice as much as white men, and that families shared the catch with young children (WB: ATSDR).

In 2012 ATSDR found no harmful radiation from eating local crops, livestock or game. It warned that eating a lot of largemouth bass, bowfin and catfish could raise mercury risks, especially for pregnant women and children. Mercury is high upstream of the site too, and ATSDR said the site's share "is not known" (WB: ATSDR).

Then budget cuts came, hitting the plant and, through it, the local economy and community. The site employed 23,351 people in 1992, about 10 percent of all jobs in six surrounding counties, with a payroll above $1.1 billion, and a 1995 DOE (Department of Energy) study warned that budget cuts could remove up to 4,200 more jobs (IA: DOE, 1995).

A study for the SRS (Savannah River Site) Community Reuse Organization, a regional development group with an interest in the site's value, counted 25,180 workers in September 1991 and 10,967 in September 2010 (IA: study for the SRS Community Reuse Organization, 2011). The counts differ by source.

The government's payments in place of taxes became a fixture. In 2008 DOE raised them from $3.5 million to $6.2 million a year (WB: DOE). GAO (Government Accountability Office) later found that Barnwell County received about $4.5 million of the $6.2 million paid in 2013, and that the land values behind the payments had been set in 1988 (WB: GAO, 2019).
Follow this thread, the towns and their economy. Earlier: Chapter 1, Living with the Plant; Chapter 2, Living with the Plant. Continues in Chapter 4, Living with the Plant.

The land recovered. By 1994 the Forest Service reported the site's red-cockaded woodpeckers had grown from 4 to 77 birds in nine years; it was restoring drained Carolina bays, round wetlands found across the region, and planting longleaf pine (DL: Forest Service, 1995).

The work to repair the land continued. Ecology laboratory scientists wrote in 2002 that cooling water had "destroyed the floodplain forests" along several streams, and that after the reactors shut down they were studying how to replant Pen Branch and Four Mile Creek. The site then held 30 set-aside research areas of 14,005 acres, and 152 woodpeckers by 1999 (IA: SREL scientists, 2002).
Follow this thread, the land and its wildlife. Earlier: Chapter 1, SRS and Ecology; Chapter 2, SRS and Ecology. Continues in Chapter 3, The Laboratories; Chapter 4, Ecology and the SRS.
The site's laboratory was named the country's newest national laboratory in 2004 (WB).

The ecology laboratory fared worse. Its grant was cut 47 percent for 2006, with layoffs that September (WB: UGA); the next year's funding fell to $1 million against an expected $4.5 million, which the site's own Citizens Advisory Board called reprehensible (WB: SRS CAB).

The House Science Committee held a hearing on it in July 2007 (DL; video IA). SREL's (Savannah River Ecology Laboratory's) web page from that summer mentions a statement on a budget crisis (WB) but the actual statement has been lost.
Follow this thread, the land and its wildlife. Earlier: Chapter 1, SRS and Ecology; Chapter 2, SRS and Ecology; Chapter 3, SRS and Ecology. Continues in Chapter 4, Ecology and the SRS.

The SRS (Savannah River Site) Museum opened in Aiken after a 2014 ribbon-cutting (WB). It is still open to the public. In November 2026 its website listed free admission, Wednesday through Saturday from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., at 224 Laurens Street SW, run by the SRS Heritage Foundation (WB: SRS Museum, 2026). The museum's first website is gone, but the Wayback Machine has it (WB). The site's archaeologists and its Cold War historic preservation program work with it (WB) — the same program that collected Ellenton's memories in 1990.

The federal record of historic engineering holds one part of the plant in detail. The Historic American Engineering Record documented the Physics Assembly Laboratory in M Area in 107 photographs and 123 data pages. It was home to the zero-power Process Development Pile, which set the physics for plutonium and tritium production in the five reactors (WB: Library of Congress, HAER SC-43).
Follow this thread, the displaced towns. Earlier: Chapter 1, The Towns Inside the Fence.

The site's weapons work is growing again. DOE (Department of Energy) decided in November 2020 to make pits, the radioactive plutonium cores of nuclear weapons, at Savannah River (WB: Federal Register), and SRS (Savannah River Site) Watch and others are challenging the decision in federal court (DL). The plant is being built by repurposing an unfinished concrete structure on the site, and in 2024 its builders were still promising it by 2032 (WB: SRS).

In 2022 NNSA (National Nuclear Security Administration) told Congress the site would not reach 50 pits a year until sometime between 2032 and 2035, not the 2030 target (IA: Congressional Research Service). In January 2023 GAO (Government Accountability Office) found that NNSA had no complete schedule or full cost estimate for pit production, and counted at least $18 billion to $24 billion in potential costs across its two pit sites (WB: GAO).

By February 2026 GAO reported the main building's possible cost at over $22 billion, up from a preliminary $6.9 billion to $11.1 billion, with completion in September 2035 at the earliest (WB: GAO 2026). NNSA's own review of 2025 said its contractor had "underperformed" on the project and been "negligent in reporting project slips" (WB: NNSA). On October 15, 2026, DOE approved the plant's baseline and authorized full construction (WB: NNSA).

Safety for the workers inside is a live question. In August 2023 the Defense Nuclear Facilities Safety Board warned that the planned controls "may not adequately protect facility workers" handling plutonium in glove boxes (WB: safety board). In May 2025 the board said NNSA's upgrades were "a significant improvement to safety" and resolved its concerns (WB: safety board).
Follow this thread, plutonium after the cold war. Earlier: Chapter 3, Plutonium: MOX and Pits. Continues in Chapter 4, Moving Plutonium Out.

South Carolina won a deal over the plutonium shipped in for the MOX (mixed oxide fuel) plant. On August 31, 2020, DOE (Department of Energy) agreed to pay the state $600 million and to remove 9.5 metric tons of plutonium by 2037; without the deal, DOE expected removal to take until 2049 (WB: DOE).

Removal works by "dilute and dispose": plutonium is mixed with other material, packed in drums and shipped to the Waste Isolation Pilot Plant in New Mexico. The site expects tens of thousands of drums over three decades (WB: SRS). In 2025 NNSA (National Nuclear Security Administration) said its contractor had beaten its targets for diluting plutonium and for shipments (WB: NNSA).

Then the policy changed. A May 2025 executive order told DOE to halt dilute and dispose, except what it owes South Carolina, and to offer surplus plutonium to industry as reactor fuel (WB: Federal Register). In March 2026 DOE said it would restart HB Line, a plutonium processing plant at H Canyon shut down a few years earlier, to recycle plutonium into reactor fuel (WB: American Nuclear Society).
Follow this thread, plutonium after the cold war. Earlier: Chapter 3, Plutonium: MOX and Pits; Chapter 4, Making Pits Again.

A new contractor, Savannah River Mission Completion, took over the liquid waste in February 2022 (WB: DOE), and DOE (Department of Energy) set a goal of closing both tank farms by 2037 (WB: DOE). The Salt Waste Processing Facility, years late, began radioactive operation in fall 2020 and passed 10 million gallons by November 2024 (WB: SRS).

The glass plant passed 4,500 canisters by its thirtieth anniversary in 2026 (WB), and in May 2026 Tank 14 became the eighth old-style tank to reach the end of waste removal in under two years (WB). Still, only 8 of the 51 tanks are formally closed, and about 32 million gallons of waste remain in the other 43 (WB: DOE).

H Canyon, the site's chemical separations plant, was set to wind down. In 2022 DOE decided to dissolve its remaining spent fuel without recovering the uranium, emptying L Basin by 2033 instead of 2060 (WB: SRS). In February 2026 DOE reversed course and restored uranium recovery, so H Canyon can make fuel for advanced reactors (WB: DOE). The site's Citizens Advisory Board has asked for briefings on what the restart means for the environment (EXT: SRS Citizens Advisory Board).
Follow this thread, waste and groundwater. Earlier: Chapter 1, Radioactive Releases; Chapter 2, Under the Ground; Chapter 3, The Tanks.

The laboratory now stands on its own. In December 2020 DOE (Department of Energy) gave Savannah River National Laboratory a separate contract, run by Battelle Savannah River Alliance (WB: DOE). On October 1, 2024, NNSA (National Nuclear Security Administration), the weapons agency, became the site's landlord, with the cleanup office as its tenant; the site then had a budget of about $3.8 billion a year and about 13,400 workers (WB: SRS).

Worker safety is still in the news. In April 2024 DOE proposed a $127,440 penalty against the main contractor after a worker lost two fingers in 2022 (WB: DOE), and in August 2026 NNSA cited it again over a thumb amputation in 2025 (WB: DOE).

On October 28, 2026, a fire at Savannah River National Laboratory led the site to declare a Site Area Emergency and close its gates to incoming traffic. The emergency ended that night, and the site said surveys found "no detectable levels of contamination" (WB: SRS). Its own releases give two different times for when the emergency was declared (EXT: SRS).

s: Sick Workers and the River Today
t: Payments to the site's sick workers keep growing. Labor Department figures show $271 million in compensation and medical bills by November 2008 (WB: Labor Department), $1.02 billion by December 2016 (WB) and $2.23 billion for 13,090 workers by April 2024 (WB). The current page lists about $3.06 billion for about 15,400 workers (WB: Labor Department).

s: Sick Workers and the River Today
t: Most cancer claims still turn on an estimate of each worker's radiation dose, and most of those fail. After NIOSH (National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health) estimated the dose, 2,271 of the site's cancer cases were accepted and 4,025 denied, and another 483 were still waiting (WB: Labor Department). In April 2026 the federal advisory board's Savannah River work group noted that a 1997 contractor check had found 79 percent of special bioassays, the samples that show whether a worker took in radioactive material, were never turned in. Its review of the main contractors' own employees was "still under consideration" (WB: NIOSH advisory board).

s: Sick Workers and the River Today
t: Tritium is still most of what the site sends into the river. In 2024 the site released 451 curies of it, and Georgia Power's Vogtle nuclear plant released 1,628. Below the site the river averaged 377 picocuries per liter, against a federal drinking-water limit of 20,000. The site put the most anyone downstream could get from drinking the water at 0.034 millirem a year, about a third of it from the site (WB: SRS).

s: Sick Workers and the River Today
t: South Carolina keeps its own watch, paid for by Energy Department grants. Its program samples drinking water that serves about 254,000 customers, and warns downstream water suppliers if tritium in the river passes trigger levels (WB: South Carolina; WB). In 2023 every drinking-water result was below federal limits, but tritium was still "the most abundant radionuclide" found (WB: South Carolina, 2023).

The payments still matter to the neighbors. When the 2022 federal budget request cut $5.7 million from them in 2021, Representative Jim Clyburn asked for the money back, and a Barnwell County council member called the payment "sort of like the sacred cow" (WB: Aiken Standard, 2021). South Carolina's 2022–23 budget spent the $525 million from the plutonium settlement, including $105 million for new schools for Williston and Blackville (WB: South Carolina budget, 2022).

Site workers still give to local charities. The contractors reported raising $1,488,038 for United Way in the 2023 campaign (WB: SRS release), and the United Way of Allendale, Bamberg and Barnwell counties called the workers' gifts "a significant portion" of its budget (WB: contractor release, 2026). Both are the contractors' own announcements.

The land the plant took is now a large managed forest, and that is the good news. The Forest Service still runs it for DOE (Department of Energy). In 2021 it thinned more than 3,000 acres, burned about 24,000 acres under control to keep the forest healthy, and sold timber from it. The red-cockaded woodpeckers kept coming back, from 3 active groups in 1985 to 150 in 2021, and golden eagles were seen on the site (WB: Forest Service, 2021). The ecology laboratory restored wetlands for the rare gopher frog in 2021 (WB: DOE), and in 2023 released the young of box turtles seized from illegal collectors (WB: DOE). The forest even helps with cleanup: a Forest Service project uses trees to draw off water contaminated with radioactive tritium, about 9.5 million gallons in 2021 (WB: Forest Service).

The bad news is that the plant's radioactivity is still in its animals. The site's deer hunts, open to the public every autumn since 1965, are still held, and every deer and hog killed is taken to a check station and tested for radioactive cesium-137 before the hunter can keep it. The site's limit is a radiation dose of 22 millirem a year to the hunter (WB: SRS, October 2026). Earlier rules said no animal is released if its radioactive cesium would put the hunter over the site's yearly radiation limit (WB: srs.gov hunt rules).

The site and its creeks stay closed to the public, fishing included. In 2021 the Forest Service replaced the trespass warning signs along thirty miles of the site's boundary on the Savannah River (WB: Forest Service).

Some fish below the site still carry radioactivity. South Carolina still advises people not to eat bowfin from the river below Stevens Creek, and notes that some fish contain radioactive cesium-137 and strontium-90 (WB: South Carolina advisory). Georgia judges its mercury limits protective enough that it sets none for radioactivity (WB: Georgia guide). The site estimated that someone eating fish from its creek mouths in 2024 would get at most about 0.24 millirem of radiation, all from cesium-137 (WB: SRS).

Much of the site's future is already planned. In 2024 it had a budget of about $3.8 billion a year and about 13,400 workers (WB: SRS). Its largest new project, the plant to make plutonium pits, was estimated in 2026 at about $22 billion, finished no sooner than September 2035 (WB: GAO 2026). DOE (Department of Energy) has promised to remove 9.5 metric tons of plutonium from South Carolina by 2037 (WB: DOE), and its cleanup contractor is to close both tank farms by the same year (WB: DOE). H Canyon is to recover uranium to make fuel for advanced reactors (WB: DOE).

The site's own record is moving. Between May and July 2026, www.srs.gov began sending visitors to a new address, public.srs.gov (WB: May 2026; WB: July 2026). Old links mostly still work, but often land on a broader page rather than the one that was linked, which is why this history cites the Wayback Machine's copies.
